mainTopic: According to רבי אליעזר, when a husband cancels his wife's vows before she makes them, do those vows take effect for a moment and then get cancelled, or do they never take effect at all?
overview: The גמרא is asking about רבי אליעזר's view that a husband can cancel his wife's vows before she makes them. Do such vows take effect for an instant and then get cancelled, or do they never take effect at all? First the גמרא shows why this matters in practice. If another person attached his vow to hers (התפסה), his vow only counts if hers ever existed. Next it tries to prove the answer from the משנה's wording 'vows that did not come into prohibition.' That proof is rejected, because the phrase can mean 'not yet.' Then it brings רבי אליעזר's קל וחומר from a person cancelling his own vows in advance. That proof is also rejected, since the two cases need not match in every way. Finally, the חכמים's reply to רבי אליעזר compares a מקוה, which cannot save pure things from becoming impure. From this the גמרא concludes that, for רבי אליעזר, pre-cancelled vows never take effect at all.

steps.title: The practical difference: someone who attached his vow to hers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why it matters whether pre-cancelled vows take effect: it decides the status of another person's vow that was attached to hers.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, where another person attached his own vow to this vow. If you say such vows take effect, then his attachment takes effect. If you say they do not take effect, then his vow has no substance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an earlier question: what practical difference does it make whether a vow that was cancelled in advance takes effect for a moment or not at all? The answer is a case where someone else attached his own vow to hers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a second person says 'my vow is like hers' (התפסה), his vow leans completely on hers. If her vow took effect even for one instant, there was something real for him to attach to, so his vow holds. If her vow never took effect at all, he attached his vow to nothing, so it is empty.

keyTerms.meaning: He attached or connected (his own vow to an existing vow)
The attachment (התפסה); a vow that takes its force from another vow
They take effect (the vows actually start to apply)
Substance, something real

steps.whyThisMatters: It turns an abstract question (did the vow exist for a moment?) into a real case with a clear practical outcome, which is why the גמרא goes on to look for an answer.

phrases.english: For example, where another person attached [his vow] to this vow.
If you say they take effect,
the attachment takes effect.
If you say they do not take effect,
there is no substance [to his vow].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the earlier question (on the previous amud) about the practical difference between the two possibilities.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference shows up when another person attached his vow to hers. If her vow took effect, his attachment holds. If not, his vow is empty.

steps.title: Proof from the משנה's wording: vows that did not come into prohibition
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the answer is and tries to prove from רבי אליעזר's words in the משנה that pre-cancelled vows never take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the answer? Come and hear: רבי אליעזר said, 'If he can cancel vows that have come into prohibition, shall he not cancel vows that have not come into prohibition?' Learn from this that such vows do not take effect.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the question matters, the גמרא asks what the answer is. It brings רבי אליעזר's own words from the משנה as a proof that pre-cancelled vows never take effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר describes advance cancellation as cancelling vows 'that did not come into prohibition.' The גמרא reads this as saying these vows never become forbidding at all, meaning they never take effect, not even for a moment.

keyTerms.meaning: What? (What is the answer to our question?)
Come and hear; introduces a source brought as a proof
Into the category of prohibition (actually forbidding something)
He cancelled (a vow); the act of הפרה
Learn from it; announces the conclusion of a proof

phrases.english: What [is the answer]? Come and hear:
Rabbi Eliezer said:
If he can cancel vows
that have come into the category of prohibition,
phrases.notes: These are vows she already made, which are already forbidding things.

phrases.english: shall he not cancel vows
that have not come into the category of prohibition?
Learn from it that they do not take effect!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי? תָּא שְׁמַע, אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the question has a practical outcome, the גמרא now tries to settle it.
steps.raayaObject: Pre-cancelled vows never take effect at all.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אליעזר's wording in the משנה: 'vows that did not come into prohibition.'

steps.title: Rejection: 'did not come' means 'not yet'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The משנה says 'have not come,' which can mean 'not yet,' not 'never come.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Does it say 'that do not come'? It says 'that have not come,' meaning they have not yet come into prohibition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof by looking closely at the exact wording רבי אליעזר used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה had said 'vows that do not come into prohibition,' that would mean they never take effect. But it says 'vows that have not come,' which only describes the moment of cancellation, before she has vowed. Once she vows, the vow could still take effect for an instant and then be cancelled, so this proof does not settle the question (step 8 does).

keyTerms.meaning: Does it teach? (Does the text actually say this?)
That do not come (never will)
Yet; still

steps.confusionAlert: The two phrases look almost the same, but 'שֶׁאֵינָן בָּאִין' would mean 'never,' while 'שֶׁלֹּא בָּאוּ' only means 'not at this moment.' The whole rejection depends on that small difference.

phrases.english: Does it teach 'that do not come'?
It teaches 'that have not come,'
[meaning] they have not yet come.
phrases.notes: So they might still take effect for a moment once she actually vows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the משנה's wording only; the question itself is still unresolved here and is settled in step 8.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof read 'have not come' as 'never come,' but it can just mean 'not yet come.'

steps.title: A second attempt: רבי אליעזר's קל וחומר from one's own vows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי אליעזר argues with a קל וחומר: a person can cancel his own vows in advance, so a husband can surely cancel his wife's vows in advance.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אליעזר said to them: A person cannot cancel his own vows after he made them, yet he can cancel them before he makes them. A husband can cancel his wife's vows after she made them, so is it not logical that he can cancel them before she makes them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a second attempt to answer the question, quoting a ברייתא from the תוספתא. This step only sets up the source; the proof drawn from it comes in step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר argues from the weaker case to the stronger one (קל וחומר). With one's own vows, cancelling afterward is impossible, yet cancelling in advance works. With a wife's vows, cancelling afterward does work, so cancelling in advance should surely work too. The comparison to one's own vows will be the key to the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And just as; opens a קל וחומר argument
His own vows
After he vowed
Before he vows
Is it not logical? The punchline of a קל וחומר

steps.whyThisMatters: By comparing advance cancellation to how a person cancels his own vows in advance, the ברייתא gives the גמרא a new way to decide whether pre-cancelled vows ever take effect.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע, אָמַר לָהֶן רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר:
phrases.english: Come and hear: Rabbi Eliezer said to them:
And just as in a situation where he cannot cancel
his own vows once he has vowed,
he can cancel his own vows
before he vows.
A situation where he can cancel his wife's vows
after she vows,
is it not logical that he should cancel his wife's vows
before she vows?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, אָמַר לָהֶן רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected, the גמרא tries a new source to answer the same question.
steps.raayaObject: Whether pre-cancelled vows take effect; the inference from this ברייתא (that they never take effect) is drawn in step 5.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in the תוספתא: רבי אליעזר's קל וחומר comparing a wife's vows to a person's own vows cancelled in advance.

steps.title: His wife's vows are like his own vows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the proof from רבי אליעזר's קל וחומר. A man's own pre-cancelled vows never take effect, so his wife's pre-cancelled vows should never take effect either.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't רבי אליעזר comparing the wife's vows to the husband's own vows? Just as his own pre-cancelled vows never take effect, her pre-cancelled vows also never take effect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the ברייתא from step 4 proves its point. It says רבי אליעזר treats the wife's vows exactly like the husband's own vows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a person cancels his own future vows in advance, the vows simply never take effect. If רבי אליעזר builds the wife's case from the husband's own case, it seems her pre-cancelled vows work the same way and never take effect either.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it that...? (the גמרא offers a reading to build a proof)
Similar to, just like
They take effect

phrases.english: Is it not
that his wife's vows are similar to his own?
Just as his own vows do not take effect at all,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets, הוא, 'he,' is part of the corrected wording. It points to the husband's own vows.

phrases.english: so too his wife's vows do not take effect at all?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof begun with the ברייתא in step 4 by drawing the inference from it.
steps.raayaObject: That pre-cancelled vows never take effect at all.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אליעזר's קל וחומר, which compares a husband's cancelling of his wife's vows to a man's cancelling of his own vows.

steps.title: The two cases do not have to be the same in every way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Each case keeps its own rule, and the קל וחומר only needs the two cases to be similar in one respect.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. His own vows work their way, and his wife's vows work their way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 5. It says the husband's own vows and his wife's vows can each follow their own rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר only needs the two cases to share the point being proven, here that cancelling in advance is possible. It does not mean they work the same way in every detail. So his own vows might never take effect, while hers might take effect for a moment and then be cancelled.

keyTerms.meaning: This one is as it is, and that one is as it is (each case keeps its own rule)

steps.confusionAlert: Comparing two cases in a קל וחומר does not make them identical. The comparison only carries over the one point being argued.

phrases.english: No, this case is as it is,
phrases.notes: "This case" is a man cancelling his own vows in advance.

phrases.english: and that case is as it is.
phrases.notes: "That case" is a husband cancelling his wife's vows in advance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only this proof. The question itself is still unresolved here; step 8 answers it.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumes the two cases in the קל וחומר must be the same in every way, but they only need to be similar on the point being proven.

steps.title: The חכמים answer רבי אליעזר with the example of a מקוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא in which the חכמים challenge רבי אליעזר's reasoning. A מקוה removes impurity but cannot protect pure things from becoming impure. So the power to change a status does not mean the power to prevent a change.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: The חכמים said to רבי אליעזר: A מקוה lifts impure people out of their impurity, yet it does not save pure people from becoming impure. A person cannot lift impure things out of their impurity. Shouldn't he surely not save pure things from becoming impure?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to answer its question. It is the חכמים's reply to רבי אליעזר's קל וחומר, and it sets up the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים say the קל וחומר is flawed. Something that can fix a status, like a מקוה, cannot necessarily block a status from starting in the first place. They prove this with a case where the kind of reasoning רבי אליעזר used would give a wrong result.

keyTerms.meaning: A ritual bath that removes impurity
Saves, protects
Raises them out of their impurity (makes them pure)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
They said to Rabbi Eliezer:
Just as a ritual bath, which raises
the impure out of their impurity,
does not save the pure from becoming impure,
then a person, who does not raise
the impure out of their impurity,
phrases.notes: This means things inside a person's body, such as something he swallowed. They are not purified when he goes into a מקוה.

phrases.english: is it not logical
that he should not save the pure from becoming impure?
phrases.notes: Yet a person really does protect what is inside him from becoming impure. So this kind of reasoning gives the wrong answer.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, אָמְרוּ לוֹ לְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the second proof (steps 4-5) was rejected in step 6, the גמרא brings a third source, a ברייתא with the חכמים's reply to רבי אליעזר, to answer the same question.
steps.raayaObject: That, in רבי אליעזר's view, pre-cancelled vows never take effect at all.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with the חכמים's reply to רבי אליעזר, based on a מקוה.

steps.title: Pre-cancelled vows never take effect
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes from the ברייתא that, in רבי אליעזר's view, vows cancelled in advance never take effect at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this that the vows do not take effect at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws its conclusion from the ברייתא in step 7. Pre-cancelled vows never take effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים compared the husband's power to "saving" pure things from ever becoming impure. That comparison only makes sense if רבי אליעזר meant the husband stops the vow from ever starting. So in his view, pre-cancelled vows never take effect at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from this (the גמרא draws a conclusion)

steps.whatToRemember: The original question was whether pre-cancelled vows take effect. The answer comes from how the חכמים argued: they treated cancelling in advance like stopping impurity before it starts. That shows the vows never take effect at all.
steps.whyThisMatters: This settles the question from step 1 about the status of another person's vow that was attached to hers. Since her vow never took effect, that attached vow has nothing to rest on.

phrases.english: Learn from this: they do not take effect!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the ברייתא brought in step 7.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In רבי אליעזר's view, vows a husband cancels in advance never take effect at all.
